lessons.title: Complementary and independent events
lessons.summary: Use complements and sample spaces and compare observed and predicted chances.
lessons.objective: Use complements and sample spaces and compare observed and predicted chances.
lessons.before: Start with all possible results. Separate those in the event from the rest.
lessons.ideas:
A probability and its complement add to 1. Subtract a known probability from 1 to find the other.

A sample-space table contains each ordered pair exactly once. For independent devices with equally likely results, all the cells are equally likely.

Divide the count of target pairs by the total number of equally likely pairs. Two totals may come from different numbers of pairs.

Choose a device and fix an event before recording. Run a small set of trials and then a larger set. Compare the fraction of successes in each with the theoretical probability.
lessons.method:
State the outcome you are finding before you calculate.

Check that both device results are represented in every cell.

Draw a short table and mark the whole diagonal of target pairs.

Compare relative frequencies when trial sets have different sizes.
mistakes: A complementary event includes every outcome outside the first event.
The first spinner’s 2 and then the second spinner’s 3 differ from the first spinner’s 3 and the second spinner’s 2.
Different possible sums are not automatically equally likely.
More trials often produce a more stable estimate. They do not guarantee an exact match in every run.

examples.title: Find a complementary probability
examples.question:
Each segment on a spinner is equally likely. The spinner has 10 segments, with 1 painted green and the others painted purple.

  1. What is the probability of not landing on green?

    [2]

  2. Why can green and not green not happen together on one spin?

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) The probability of green is \(\frac{1}{10}\). Green and not green include every result, so their probabilities add to 1.

Subtract \(\frac{1}{10}\) from 1.

\(\frac{9}{10}\)

(b) The two events are mutually exclusive and they cover all outcomes.

Each landing is on one segment with just one colour.

examples.title: An outcome from each of two independent spinners
examples.question:
One fair spinner is numbered 1 to 2. A separate fair spinner is numbered 1 to 4. Spin each once.

  1. How many ordered pairs of outcomes are possible?

    [2]

  2. Find the probability that both results are 2.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) Each of the 2 first outcomes can be combined with any of the 4 second outcomes.

This makes a rectangular sample space.

\(8\)

(b) The one favourable pair is (2, 2). The 8 ordered pairs are equally likely.

\(\frac{1}{8}\)

examples.title: Find a sum from two independent spinners
examples.question:
A fair spinner shows an integer from 1 to 12. Another fair spinner shows an integer from 1 to 4. Spin both and add the results.

  1. Find the chance that the sum is 14.

    [2]

  2. Explain why the smallest sum and a sum near the middle may have different probabilities.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) There are 48 equally likely pairs. The pairs giving the target are (10, 4), (11, 3), (12, 2).

Count the favourable pairs and divide by the total.

\(\frac{1}{16}\)

(b) Find a pair that gives the smallest sum and try to make the same sum another way.

Several ordered pairs can give a middle sum, whereas 2 comes only from (1, 1).

examples.title: Compare experimental results with a model
examples.question:
A fair spinner is half blue. Two groups make separate sets of spins.
Trial setSpinsLanded on blue
A4025
B16081

  1. Find the experimental probability of blue in set A.

    [2]

  2. Which set gives a result closer to the theoretical probability? Show how you decided.

    [2]

  3. Design one more fair simulation to compare a small trial and a large trial.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) In set A there are 25 blue outcomes out of 40 spins.

\(\frac{5}{8}\)

(b) Use proportions rather than comparing the raw counts. A larger trial set often gives a closer result, though it is not guaranteed.

Set B. Its estimate is \(\frac{81}{160}\), closer to one half than \(\frac{5}{8}\).

(c) Find the two success fractions and compare both with one half. A larger experiment does not guarantee a closer result every time.

Toss a fair coin. Mark heads as success. Use the same coin for both trials. Choose two group sizes before starting and record every result.

questions.title: Find a complementary probability
questions.prompt_html:
Each segment on a spinner is equally likely. The spinner has 11 segments, with 9 painted green and the others painted purple.

  1. What is the probability of not landing on green?

    [2]

  2. Why can green and not green not happen together on one spin?

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a) \(\frac{2}{11}\)

(b) Each landing is on one segment with just one colour.
questions.solution_html:
(a) The probability of green is \(\frac{9}{11}\). Green and not green include every result, so their probabilities add to 1.

Subtract \(\frac{9}{11}\) from 1.

\(\frac{2}{11}\)

(b) The two events are mutually exclusive and they cover all outcomes.

Each landing is on one segment with just one colour.
questions.hint_html: Subtract the known probability from 1.

marking_criteria.description_html: Each landing is on one segment with just one colour.

questions.title: An outcome from each of two independent spinners
questions.prompt_html:
One fair spinner is numbered 1 to 9. A separate fair spinner is numbered 1 to 6. Spin each once.

  1. How many ordered pairs of outcomes are possible?

    [2]

  2. Find the probability that both results are 2.

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
(a) Each of the 9 first outcomes can be combined with any of the 6 second outcomes.

This makes a rectangular sample space.

\(54\)

(b) The one favourable pair is (2, 2). The 54 ordered pairs are equally likely.

\(\frac{1}{54}\)
questions.hint_html: Multiply the two counts of possible outcomes.

marking_criteria.description_html: Multiply the two counts of possible outcomes.
Divide the count of favourable pairs by the total.
